threads.topic: What happened to the LOBOs on 22 July

entries.q: The outturn report went to Cabinet on 21 July saying the LOBO call right 'may be exercised at the next call date, July 2026'. That date was 22 July. Was the option exercised on the £19.25m, and if the loans were repaid, at what rate were they replaced?
entries.why: The LOBOs cost 4.65%. PWLB 10-year is currently around 6%. On £19.25m that is roughly £264,000 a year, and it will have been decided before this committee next sits.

entries.q: Wolverhampton reports three LOBO calls in 2025-26 where lenders proposed 6.19%, 6.21% and 6.26% against existing rates of 3.60%, 4.26% and 4.29%. It rejected all three and repaid £17.0m, having built the possibility into its cashflow in advance.
entries.why: That is the shape of the decision Bridgend faced on 22 July on £19.25m at 4.65%. A lender calling is generally offering a rate set to be refused, so the practical question is whether the cash was ready to repay — not whether the new rate was acceptable.

threads.topic: Two thirds of the cash is lent to other councils

entries.q: £30.00m of £44.50m of investments — 67% — sits with other local authorities, none of which carry a credit rating. What is the largest single exposure, and what would trigger a reduction in the local authority allocation?
entries.why: The strategy relies on councils being secure counterparties. That is generally right and has never been tested at a section 114 authority, which is precisely why the concentration limit matters more than the average rate.

entries.q: 2026-27 carries £30.37m of indicated new borrowing, £7.79m of maturing PWLB debt and potentially £19.25m of called LOBOs — close to £57m of borrowing decisions in one year, against a book that currently averages 4.63%. What rate does the MTFS assume, and what does each 1% above it cost?
entries.why: The council's own indicator puts a 1% rise at £432,000 of annual revenue. Three separate refinancings in one year is not three separate risks — it is one, taken three times.

threads.topic: The internal borrowing is running out of cash

entries.q: Balance sheet resources fall from £124.24m to £80.46m and then £63.19m over three years while the loans CFR rises from £169.69m to £193.26m. The liability benchmark more than doubles as a result. Is that fall in reserves a plan or a forecast?
entries.why: The liability benchmark moves on two assumptions — capital spend and reserves — and the reserves assumption is doing most of the work here. If reserves hold up, the borrowing need is smaller than £140m; if they fall faster, it is larger.

summary.text:
A Welsh unitary whose treasury reporting is among the clearest we have read — and which has a decision sitting in it that the paper itself flags and does not resolve. At 31 March 2026 Bridgend held £99.72m of external borrowing against a £182.56m capital financing requirement, leaving £69.97m borrowed internally from its own balances. The whole book costs an average 4.63%.

£19.25m of it is LOBO debt — three loans taken in January 2004, carried at 4.65%, nominally running to 2054. The lender can reset the rate every January and July, and the council can refuse, which forces repayment. The outturn report, written for the year to 31 March and taken to Cabinet on 21 July, says plainly that the right 'may be exercised at the next call date, July 2026' and that the council 'will need to consider taking out new debt to replace them'. That date was 22 July — the day after Cabinet. The council's own maturity table already treats the whole £19.25m as due within twelve months, which is why 27.32% of the book sits in the under-one-year bucket.

The arithmetic of replacing it is not subtle. The LOBOs cost 4.65%. The PWLB 10-year maturity rate struck at 6.02% this morning. On £19.25m that difference is roughly £264,000 a year, and the paper does not put a figure on it.

Investments are £44.50m, up from £36.75m, earning 4.73% at year end. £30.00m of that — 67% — is lent to other local authorities, at a weighted 5.29%, picked up over the year-end period when the council-to-council market pays best. Nothing is placed beyond 364 days. It is a deliberate and well-executed position; it is also two thirds of the portfolio in a sector whose credit story is the reason anyone reads these papers.

The direction of travel is the familiar one. The CFR rises from £182.56m to £203.77m in 2026-27, balance sheet resources fall from £124.24m to £80.46m and then £63.19m, and the liability benchmark — the least the council must borrow — goes from £55.45m to £121.90m to £140.07m across the same three years. Against that, £30.37m of new borrowing is indicated for 2026-27, before the £19.25m of LOBOs and the £7.79m of PWLB debt maturing in the same year are refinanced. MRP is already £6.508m.

officer.subject: Your Governance and Audit Committee on 24 September — the LOBO call date has passed
officer.body:
Dear Colleague,

Your Governance and Audit Committee meets on Thursday 24 September, and your own treasury outturn report names it as the committee responsible for scrutinising the strategy. We read council treasury papers and track PWLB rates every working day. We have been through Bridgend's outturn to 31 March 2026, which went to Cabinet on 21 July.

It is one of the clearest treasury reports we have read this year — the liability benchmark table, the maturity structure and the counterparty detail are all there and they reconcile. This is not a list of things missing. It is the shortlist of questions we would expect a member who has read it properly to put to you.

The one with a date on it. Your report says the LOBO call right "may be exercised at the next call date, July 2026" and that the council "will need to consider taking out new debt to replace them". The report went to Cabinet on 21 July; the call date was 22 July, the day after. Whatever happened will have happened before this committee next sits, and the report as published leaves members without the answer.

The arithmetic is the part worth having ready. The £19.25m of LOBOs carries 4.65%. The PWLB 10-year maturity rate struck at 6.02% this morning, notice 309/26; 25-year at 6.65%. If the loans were called and replaced at around current levels, that is roughly £264,000 a year on £19.25m — against a whole-book average of 4.63% and total interest payable of £5.851m in 2025-26. A member who does that sum will want to know whether it lands in the MTFS.

Three we would expect beyond that:

1. On the refinancing load. 2026-27 carries £30.37m of indicated new borrowing on the liability benchmark, £7.79m of maturing PWLB debt, and potentially the £19.25m of LOBOs — close to £57m of borrowing decisions in a single year. Your own indicator puts a 1% rise at £432,000 of annual revenue. Expect to be asked what rate the MTFS assumes and what each 1% above it costs.

2. On the counterparty concentration. £30.00m of the £44.50m investment book — 67% — sits with other local authorities at a weighted 5.29%. The year-end timing is well judged and the return shows it. The question is the size of the largest single exposure and what would trigger a reduction, because local authorities are the one counterparty class that carries no rating and the sector's credit story is the reason anyone reads these papers.

3. On the liability benchmark's reserves assumption. Balance sheet resources fall from £124.24m to £80.46m and then £63.19m across the forecast, which is what takes the benchmark from £55.45m to £121.90m to £140.07m. Members will reasonably ask whether that fall is a plan or a forecast, because it is doing more work in the borrowing number than the capital programme is.

Every figure above is from Bridgend's own report or from today's PWLB fixing, and we will send page references for any of them.

A word on who we are, since this arrived unasked. PWLBtoday tracks PWLB rates every working day and reads the treasury papers of every council that publishes them. We do not sell treasury products and we do not advise on borrowing. There is a training library alongside it, for officers and for members. The courses your papers point to are listed with this email, each with the figure that put it there.

With best wishes,

PWLBtoday
pwlbtoday.org

member.subject: Your committee meets 24 September — £19.25m of loans may have been called on 22 July
member.body:
Dear Councillor,

Your Governance and Audit Committee meets on Thursday 24 September, and the council's own treasury report names your committee as the one responsible for scrutinising this. We read council treasury papers and track PWLB borrowing rates every working day, and we have read Bridgend's.

We should say at the outset that it is a good report — clearer than most, and the officers have set out the position properly. This is not a complaint. There is simply one question in it with a date attached, and that date has passed.

The council has £19.25m of a type of loan called a LOBO — Lender's Option, Borrower's Option. Three of them, taken in January 2004, currently costing 4.65%. The lender is allowed to change the interest rate twice a year. If they do, the council can refuse, but refusing means repaying the loan immediately and borrowing the money again somewhere else.

Your report, which went to Cabinet on 21 July, says the lender's right "may be exercised at the next call date, July 2026". That date was 22 July — the day after Cabinet met. **Was the option exercised, and if the loans were repaid, what rate replaced them?**

This matters because of the price difference. The LOBOs cost 4.65%. Councils currently borrow from the government's Public Works Loan Board at around 6% for ten years — it struck at 6.02% this morning. On £19.25m, that gap is roughly £264,000 a year, every year. The report does not put that number in front of you, and the decision will have been taken before your committee next meets.

Two other things worth asking about.

**How much borrowing is being done next year, all told?** The council's own figures point to £30.37m of new borrowing in 2026-27, plus £7.79m of existing loans falling due, plus possibly the £19.25m of LOBOs. That is close to £57m of borrowing decisions in one year, against a debt book that currently averages 4.63%. The report says a 1% rise in rates costs the council £432,000 a year.

**Where is the council's spare cash?** Bridgend holds £44.50m of investments. £30.00m of it — two thirds — is lent to other local authorities. That is normal, it is legal, and it earned a good return. It is also the one type of borrower that carries no credit rating, so it is worth knowing what the largest single loan to another council is.

One piece of context. The council currently uses £69.97m of its own cash instead of borrowing — sensible while the cash is there. The report forecasts that cash falling from £124m to £80m and then £63m over three years. That fall, more than the building programme, is what drives the borrowing figures above.

Every figure here comes from Bridgend's own published report or from today's PWLB rate, and we are happy to send page references for all of them.

A word on who we are, since this arrived unasked. PWLBtoday tracks PWLB rates every working day and reads the treasury papers of every council that publishes them. We do not sell treasury products, we do not advise councils on borrowing, and we have no view on what Bridgend should do — which is why we can put the numbers and the questions in front of you and leave the judgement to you. There is also a training library, including short courses written for members rather than accountants — one of them on exactly the kind of loan described above.

If any of this is useful, or if you want the page references, just reply.

With best wishes,

PWLBtoday
pwlbtoday.org
